bibliographic.authors: Jiun-Horng Tsai, Yung-Chen Yao, Pei-Hsiu Huang, Hung-Lung Chiang (corresponding)
bibliographic.title: Fuel Economy and Volatile Organic Compound Exhaust Emission for Motorcycles with Various Running Mileages
bibliographic.volumeIssuePages: 18: 3056-3067 (PDF p.1-12; journal page = PDF page + 3055). Received 16 July 2018, revised 12 Oct 2018, accepted 19 Nov 2018
bibliographic.funding: No funding or acknowledgements statement printed in the text.
bibliographic.openAccess: unknown (copyright Taiwan Association for Aerosol Research; no licence statement in the PDF)
bibliographic.citation: Tsai J-H, Yao Y-C, Huang P-H, Chiang H-L (2018). Fuel Economy and Volatile Organic Compound Exhaust Emission for Motorcycles with Various Running Mileages. Aerosol and Air Quality Research 18:3056-3067. doi:10.4209/aaqr.2018.07.0264

studyDesign: Chassis-dynamometer laboratory study of 43 in-use four-stroke gasoline motorcycles in Taiwan (no electric vehicles). 7 phase III (mean age 15.0 +/- 3.6 y; 45,613 +/- 11,947 km), 16 phase IV (8.2 +/- 1.8 y; 30,120 +/- 9,067 km), 20 phase V (4.0 +/- 1.5 y; 12,179 +/- 6,337 km). Engine sizes, model years and scooter/gear split not reported. Regrouped by mileage into six groups (text says seven): <=10,000 n=6; 10,001-15,000 n=8; 15,001-20,000 n=8; 20,001-30,000 n=8; 30,001-40,000 n=6; >40,001 n=7. ECE cycle, 780 s (240 s idle); room 25-30 C; 95-octane fuel with 10.2% MTBE, 30.0 vol% aromatics, 0.52% benzene; fuel replaced and engine cooled before each test. HORIBA CVS-51S whole-cycle bag sampling; NDIR, FID, chemiluminescence; purge-and-trap GC/MS (52 VOCs) and DNPH-HPLC (15 carbonyls); OFP via Carter (2009) MIR; two-way ANOVA with Scheffe test. Emission factors are per litre of fuel burned (g/L), not per km. Everything is tailpipe emission in a laboratory; nothing is measured on a street, in air, on people or in health outcomes. OFP is computed, not measured.

findings.claim: The study tested 43 in-use four-stroke gasoline motorcycles of three emission-regulation phases on a chassis dynamometer.
findings.value: n = 7 (phase III), 16 (phase IV), 20 (phase V); mean age 15.0/8.2/4.0 y; mean mileage 45,613/30,120/12,179 km
findings.page: PDF p.2 (journal 3057); fuel and test details PDF p.3 (journal 3058)
findings.quote: Seven motorcycles were classified as regulation phase III
findings.caveats: Small samples, especially phase III (n=7). Engine capacities, model years, and whether the bikes are scooters (CVT) or manual-gear motorcycles are not reported. Cross-sectional: bikes differ in phase, age and mileage together.
findings.useOnSite: Based on 43 in-use gasoline motorcycles tested on a laboratory dynamometer in Taiwan.
findings.checkerNote: Reader cited PDF p.3 for journal p.3057; journal 3057 is PDF p.2 (journal page = PDF page + 3055). Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: Fuel economy was lowest in the oldest (phase III) motorcycles and highest in phase V.
findings.caveats: Table 1 prints 29.5 +/- 2.46, 32.6 +/- 1.85, 34.7 +/- 1.45. Phase III is 15% below phase V and phase IV 6.2% below V (text). Phases differ in age and mileage as well as regulation.
findings.significance: Table 1: IV and V p<0.05 vs III (*); V vs IV also p<0.05 (#)
findings.useOnSite: Older motorcycles in the test covered about 15% fewer km per litre than newer ones.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers, asterisks and # markers verified on PDF p.4 image.

findings.claim: Carbon monoxide emitted per litre of fuel was much higher for older-phase motorcycles.
findings.caveats: Table 1 prints the phase III SD as 71 (the trailing '2' is a footnote marker) while the text prints 74; the paper is internally inconsistent. Per litre of fuel, not per km. Phase III n=7. Phase III is older and higher mileage, so age/wear is confounded with regulation phase.
findings.significance: p<0.05 for IV and V vs III (Table 1 *); IV vs V also significant (#)
findings.useOnSite: Phase III motorcycles emitted about 2.6 times the CO per litre of fuel of phase V motorcycles in this test.
findings.checkerNote: Reader called the table value garbled '712'; it is 71 with a superscript footnote 2. Text says 74. Quote fixed. Ratio 216/84.3 = 2.56 checks with +156%.

findings.claim: Total hydrocarbon (HC) emission per litre of fuel was higher for older motorcycles, but phase IV and V did not differ significantly.
findings.caveats: Table 1 gives integers; one-decimal values come from the text. No # on the phase V HC cell, consistent with the text saying IV vs V HC is not significant. Per litre of fuel.
findings.significance: III vs IV and III vs V p<0.05; IV vs V p>0.05
findings.useOnSite: Phase III motorcycles emitted about 1.8 times the hydrocarbons per litre of fuel of phase V ones; phase IV and V were not statistically different.
findings.checkerNote: Verified against Table 1 image and text.

findings.claim: NOx and CO2 per litre of fuel were LOWER in the older motorcycles.
findings.caveats: Newer bikes emit more NOx per litre, which complicates an 'old = dirtier on everything' story. NOx III vs IV is not significant (no asterisk on IV). The paper attributes the NOx fall to 'combustion efficiency'; the explanation that low CO2 reflects incomplete combustion is the reader's inference, not printed.
findings.significance: V vs III p<0.05 for NOx and CO2; V vs IV p<0.05 (#); IV vs III not significant for NOx or CO2
findings.useOnSite: Older motorcycles emitted more CO and hydrocarbons but somewhat less NOx per litre of fuel.
findings.checkerNote: Added CO2 SD table/text mismatch, significance pattern, and flagged the incomplete-combustion explanation as not in the paper.

findings.claim: The paper reports emission factors per litre of fuel only; it gives no g/km and no comparison with regulatory limits.
findings.value: All factors in g per litre of fuel (g/L)
findings.quote: Exhaust emission (g L–1) and fuel economy (km L–1) for various motorcycles
findings.caveats: A g/km figure could only be derived by dividing mean g/L by mean km/L (phase V CO 84.3/34.7 = about 2.4 g/km); this is checker arithmetic on means, not a paper result, and is not recommended for publication.
findings.useOnSite: Do not quote these figures as g/km or as 'exceeding the legal limit'; the paper gives neither.
findings.checkerNote: Reader labelled this 'author-opinion'; it is an omission (the paper is silent), so kind changed. Content otherwise confirmed.

findings.claim: Fuel economy fell with accumulated mileage.
findings.page: PDF p.5 (journal 3060); Fig. 2 PDF p.5; Conclusion PDF p.10 (journal 3065)
findings.quote: a reduction rate of about 1.3 km L–1 per 10,000 km
findings.caveats: Cross-sectional comparison of different motorcycles, not the same bikes tracked over time; age, mileage and phase are confounded. Fig. 2 plots boxes by regulation phase against mean mileage; the 35.5 and 29.9 km/L end-point values appear only in the text.
findings.significance: Fig. 2 inset gives r2 = 0.60 (individual bikes, fuel economy vs running mileage); no p-value
findings.useOnSite: In this fleet, higher-mileage motorcycles used more fuel per km.
findings.checkerNote: Reader said no fit statistic for Fig. 2; the figure inset prints r2=0.60. Page corrected (journal 3060 = PDF p.5). (35.5-29.9)/35.5 = 15.8%, consistent with 16%.

findings.claim: CO emission per litre rose about 3.3-fold with mileage across the tested fleet.
findings.page: Text PDF p.5 (journal 3060); Fig. 3(a) PDF p.6 (journal 3061); Conclusion PDF p.10
findings.quote: the average CO emission was 61 ± 30 g L–1 at 5,231 ± 4,353 km, increasing to 203 ± 75 g L–1
findings.caveats: r2 is on six group means (six points in Fig. 3), which flatters the fit. Group means are not monotonic: the 30-40k group (about 123 g/L by eye) is below the 20-30k group (about 147). No test of the CO trend is given. Slope check: 34 x 4.24 = 144 vs 203-61 = 142.
findings.significance: r2 = 0.87 (group means); no CI or p
findings.useOnSite: In the test, CO per litre rose roughly three-fold from low-mileage to high-mileage motorcycles.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers confirmed; page references fixed (text is PDF p.5, figure PDF p.6).

findings.claim: HC emission per litre rose 1.7-fold with mileage and was significantly higher only above 30,000 km.
findings.page: Text PDF p.5 (journal 3060); Fig. 3(b) PDF p.6; Conclusion PDF p.10
findings.quote: Hydrocarbon emission increased significantly (p-value < 0.05) at running mileages of over 30,000 km
findings.caveats: The text does not say what the 30,000 km groups were compared against (presumably the lowest-mileage group). Catalyst failure is the authors' suggested explanation; catalyst condition was not measured. Group means non-monotonic: 20-30k group about 28 g/L is below the 15-20k group (about 32). r2 on six group means.
findings.useOnSite: Hydrocarbon emissions per litre rose significantly once motorcycles passed about 30,000 km.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected; added unstated comparator and non-monotonic group means.

findings.claim: NOx per litre decreased with mileage.
findings.page: Text PDF p.5; Fig. 3(c) PDF p.6; Conclusion PDF p.10
findings.quote: the NOx emission (Fig. 3(c)) decreased with increasing mileage
findings.caveats: Opposite direction to CO/HC; the authors attribute it to 'combustion efficiency'. r2 on six group means.
findings.useOnSite: NOx fell with mileage while CO and hydrocarbons rose.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers confirmed; page references fixed.

findings.claim: Total of 67 VOCs per litre of fuel was about 25 g/L at the lowest mileage and 47 g/L at the highest, but only the >40,000 km group differed significantly from the <10,000 km group.
findings.value: 47.1 +/- 19.8 g/L at 47,617 km; low-mileage value printed as 25.2 +/- 8.0 g/L in the abstract but 19.1 +/- 9.7 g/L in the text (PDF p.5); Fig. 4 bar for <10,000 km is about 25 g/L; increase 6.61 g/L per 10,000 km
findings.page: PDF p.1 (abstract), p.5-8 (journal 3060-3063); Fig. 4 PDF p.7
findings.quote: For running mileages of over 40,000 km, paraffins, olefins, aromatics, carbonyls, and total of 67 VOCs emissions significantly increased (p-value < 0.05)
findings.caveats: INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. Fig. 4 (stacked bars, about 25 g/L at <10,000 km and about 47 at >40,000 km) agrees with the abstract's 25.2. The text's 19.1 agrees with the slope (47.1 - 6.61 x 4.24 = 19.1), so it looks like a fitted value, but the paper does not say so. Using the observed bars the rise is about 1.9-fold, not 2.5-fold. Within 40,000 km the rise was not significant (p>0.05); the 15-20k group (about 22 g/L) fell below the lowest group; the 30-40k bar (about 39 g/L) was not flagged significant.
findings.significance: p<0.05 only for >40,000 km vs <10,000 km
findings.useOnSite: VOC output per litre of fuel roughly doubled (about 25 to about 47 g/L) in the highest-mileage motorcycles (over 40,000 km); below that the trend was not statistically significant.
findings.checkerNote: Reader said the low value was uncertain; Fig. 4 resolves it toward 25 (abstract). Bar heights are visual estimates. Recommend publishing 25 -> 47 with the caveat, or only the >40,000 km figure.

findings.claim: Exhaust VOC mass was mostly aromatics and paraffins, with olefins and a few percent carbonyls.
findings.value: Paraffins 38-45%, olefins 9.7-15%, aromatics 38-48%, carbonyls 1.8-3.0% of VOC mass across mileage groups; paraffins plus aromatics over 80%
findings.quote: paraffins (38–45%), olefins (9.7–15%), aromatics (38–48%), and carbonyls (1.8–3.0%)
findings.caveats: Percentages are of the 67 analysed VOCs only (52 GC/MS species plus 15 carbonyls), not of all hydrocarbons; heavier or unidentified compounds are excluded.
findings.useOnSite: Roughly four-tenths of the measured VOC mass in the exhaust was aromatic compounds such as benzene, toluene and xylenes.
findings.checkerNote: Verified in text and abstract.

findings.claim: Group emission factors: paraffins 9.0-19, olefins 2.2-5.7, aromatics 8.9-22, carbonyls 0.41-0.80 g per litre (text values for 5,231 to 47,617 km).
findings.value: Text: paraffins 9.0-19; olefins 2.2 to 5.7; aromatics 8.9 to 22; 15 carbonyls 0.41 to 0.80 g/L. Fold increase 5,231 to 47,617 km: paraffins 2.45, olefins 2.52, aromatics 2.49, carbonyls 1.92. Per 10,000 km: paraffins 2.60, olefins 0.81, aromatics 3.11, carbonyls 0.08 g/L.
findings.quote: total aromatics ranging from 8.9 to 22 g L–1 for average running mileages of 5,231 to 47,617 km
findings.caveats: The low-end text values do not match the first bars of Figs 5(b) and 5(c): the <10,000 km olefin bar is about 3.0 g/L (text 2.2) and the aromatic bar about 11.4 g/L (text 8.9); paraffins about 10.5 (text 9.0). The text minima look like fitted or lowest-group values. The high end (18.7 paraffin, 5.7 olefin, 22 aromatic) matches the >40,000 km bars. No species-by-mileage table is printed; Fig. 5(d) (carbonyls) is cited but absent from the PDF. Asterisks: only >40,000 km in Figs 4, 5(b), 5(c); 30-40k and >40k in Fig. 5(a).
findings.significance: Significant vs <10,000 km group (*) as stated above
findings.useOnSite: Aromatics reached about 22 g per litre of fuel in the >40,000 km group; do not publish the low-mileage group values as measured.
findings.checkerNote: Added the text-versus-figure mismatch at the low end and the 5(a) significance marker on the 30-40k group. Fold increases in the text probably use the same low values.

findings.claim: Toluene, isopentane, xylenes, 1-butene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, ethylbenzene, n-pentane and benzene were the main VOCs in the exhaust.
findings.value: Species list only. Dominant aromatics (toluene, m,p-xylene, o-xylene, trimethylbenzene, m-ethyltoluene, ethylbenzene, benzene) = 68-79% of analysed aromatics; paraffins: isopentane, n-pentane, 2,3-dimethylbutane, 3-methylpentane, n-decane, n-undecane; olefins 1-butene, propene, isoprene, 1-hexene = 70-82% of olefins; carbonyls (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone, butyraldehyde, benzaldehyde, isovaleraldehyde, valeraldehyde) = 78-84%.
findings.quote: Toluene, isopentane, m,p-xylene, o-xylene, 1-butene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, ethylbenzene, n-pentane, and benzene were the main VOCs in motorcycle exhaust.
findings.caveats: No numeric emission factor for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene or xylenes is printed. By eye in Fig. 5(c), benzene is the thin bottom segment (about 0.7-1 g/L) and toluene about 2-5 g/L; these are visual estimates only. 1,3-butadiene is not reported; formaldehyde has no printed mass value. Reader's page '1, 7' ok; reader's 'text p.3061' should be journal 3062.
findings.useOnSite: Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylenes were among the main compounds in the exhaust; the paper does not give a benzene number.
findings.checkerNote: Added the paraffin species list and the visual-estimate caveat; page fixed.

findings.claim: The test fuel was commercial 95-octane unleaded gasoline with 0.52% benzene and 30 vol% aromatics.
findings.value: Benzene 0.52%; aromatics 30.0 vol%; olefins 10.8%; paraffins 10.7%; naphthenes 6.1%; MTBE 10.2%; oxygen 1.8 wt%
findings.quote: benzene content was 0.52%
findings.caveats: The unit basis (vol or wt) for benzene is not stated. Exhaust aromatics partly come from fuel aromatics and partly from combustion chemistry (authors discuss formation). One fuel only. Market fuel today may differ.
findings.useOnSite: The test gasoline contained 0.52% benzene and 30 vol% aromatics.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Computed ozone formation potential (OFP) of the exhaust VOCs about doubled with mileage.
findings.locator: Table 2 last row; text p.3064; Conclusion
findings.caveats: OFP is computed (mass x Carter MIR factor), not measured, and describes ozone/smog formation, not direct toxicity to pedestrians. The text gives 90.7-112 for the first four groups (Table 2: 91-111) and mean mileages 26,715, 36,615 and 48,917 km, which differ from the group means on the Fig. 4 axis (about 26,720; 36,230; 47,620). The text says OFP 'significantly increased' for 174 and 204 but gives no test statistic.
findings.useOnSite: Computed ozone-forming potential of the exhaust roughly doubled between low- and high-mileage motorcycles.
findings.checkerNote: Table 2 numbers verified on PDF p.10 image.

findings.claim: Aromatics contribute the largest share of ozone-forming potential.
findings.value: Text: aromatics 50-67%, olefins 22-34%, paraffins 10-13%, carbonyls 2-3%. Table 2 >40,001 km group (g-O3/L): aromatics 126, olefins 52, paraffins 23, carbonyls 3.5 (of 204).
findings.quote: 10–13% for paraffins, 22–34% for olefins, 50–67% for aromatics, and 2–3% for carbonyls
findings.caveats: Shares computed from Table 2 group rows: aromatics 50-67%, olefins 21-34%, paraffins 10-13.5%, carbonyls 1.6-2.6%. Table-derived values sit at or slightly outside the text ranges for olefins and carbonyls.
findings.useOnSite: Aromatics such as xylenes, toluene and trimethylbenzenes account for most of the exhaust's ozone-forming potential.
findings.checkerNote: Reader said olefin shares were about 25-28%; the table gives 21-34% (30-40k group 21%, 20-30k group 34%). Carbonyl range corrected.

findings.claim: Individual high-OFP species include xylenes, toluene, 1-butene, trimethylbenzenes, isoprene and propene.
findings.value: Average OFP g-O3/L (text): m,p-xylene 13.0; o-xylene 9.6; toluene 10.5; 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene 10.3; 1,2,3-TMB 8.1; 1,3,5-TMB 6.3; ethyltoluene 6.8; 1-butene 13.7; isoprene 11.7; propene 7.7; 1-hexene 7.4. Table 2 >40,001 km: toluene 18.18, m,p-xylene 20.82, 1,2,4-TMB 18.77, 1-butene 13.67. Formaldehyde 0.47-1.18; acetaldehyde 0.58-0.97; ethylbenzene 1.86-3.86.
findings.caveats: Benzene is not among the 20 species in Table 2, so it is a minor ozone contributor by this metric even though it is a priority toxic; OFP says nothing about toxicity. Table 2 prints C9H13 for ethyltoluene (should be C9H12 as for the other C9 aromatics). m,p-xylene is highest in the 30-40k group (25.70), above the >40k group.
findings.useOnSite: OFP is a smog metric; the paper does not rank species by toxicity.
findings.checkerNote: Reader gave ethylbenzene OFP as 2.07-3.86; the table minimum is 1.86 (20-30k group). Other numbers verified.

findings.claim: The authors suggest incomplete combustion and catalyst failure explain higher HC at high mileage but did not test the catalyst.
findings.quote: which may be attributed to incomplete combustion and failure of the catalyst system
findings.caveats: Speculation; no catalyst, maintenance or air-fuel data reported.
findings.useOnSite: The authors suggest ageing emission controls may play a part.
findings.checkerNote: Only the page changed (reader had PDF p.6; the sentence is on PDF p.5).

findings.claim: The ECE test cycle includes 240 s of idle out of 780 s, but results are whole-cycle totals, so idle emissions are not separated.
findings.quote: including 240 seconds for the idle stage
findings.caveats: No idle-only, cold-start-only or mode-resolved data; no data at tailpipe height, crosswalks or street air. The paper cannot support 'low to the ground' or 'at the red light' claims.
findings.useOnSite: This paper gives whole-cycle exhaust totals only; it does not separate idle.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. Intro mentions idle testing of in-use bikes as regulation but reports no idle data.

findings.claim: Taiwan's regulatory test changed from hot start to cold start in January 2004; the paper cites that gasoline cars can emit 5-10 times more NMHC at cold start.
findings.value: 5-10 times higher NMHC for cold vs warm start (light-duty gasoline vehicles, citing May et al. 2014)
findings.page: PDF p.2 (journal 3057, 2004 change); PDF p.9 (journal 3064, 5-10 times)
findings.quote: gasoline vehicles can emit over 5–10 times higher NMHC during a cold start compared to a warm start
findings.caveats: Cited from a study of cars, not measured here. The paper never states whether its own tests were cold start (engine was cooled overnight).
findings.useOnSite: Do not attribute the cold-start figure to this paper's own measurements.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's page '3, 9' fixed to PDF p.2 and p.9.

findings.claim: Motorcycles were reported to contribute 19.6% of CO, 10.6% of HC and 2.6% of NOx emissions in Taiwan (TEPA 2013).
findings.quote: Motorcycles contribute approximately 19.6% (178,700 ton yr–1) of CO emission
findings.caveats: From the TEPA (2013) inventory; the data year is not given in the paper.
findings.useOnSite: Cite as TEPA 2013 via Tsai et al., not as a Tsai finding.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: 74% of motorcycles in Taiwan are four-stroke; two-stroke production ended in 2004.
findings.quote: 74% of motorcycles in Taiwan have four-stroke engines
findings.caveats: From TEPA (2013). The sentence 'More than 60% of motorcycle emissions are now contributed by four-stroke engines' carries no citation.
findings.useOnSite: Tested bikes were four-stroke, the majority type in Taiwan.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The paper states in general terms that many VOCs are hazardous or toxic and that reactive aromatics (toluene, xylenes) drive ozone formation, without health data of its own.
findings.quote: many VOCs have been identified as hazardous or toxic air pollutants
findings.caveats: One sentence with a citation (Perez-Rial et al. 2010). No exposure, health, pedestrian or child data.
findings.useOnSite: Not usable as evidence of health effects.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Taiwan's in-use motorcycle inspection: annual periodic inspection for motorcycles older than five years, plus random roadside hot-spot inspections.
findings.quote: motorcycles older than five years are inspected annually at a certified testing station
findings.caveats: Description of the system; the paper does not evaluate its effectiveness beyond noting motorcycles remain a major urban source.
findings.useOnSite: Context only.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The paper cites fuel-economy standards (Taiwan 38 km/L for 100-150 cc after 2011) but prints no phase-specific CO/HC/NOx emission limits.
findings.value: Taiwan fuel-economy standard 36 and 39 km/L (2002-2010), 38 km/L (from 2011); in-use fuel consumption can be 10-30% above standard; regulation phase VI (following Euro 4) as of 2017; guaranteed mileage 6,000 km (1991), 15,000 km (1998), 20,000 km (2017)
findings.quote: the fuel economy standard was set at 38 km L–1 for 100- to 150-cc engine capacities
findings.locator: Introduction; Results p.3059; Test Procedures p.3057
findings.caveats: Tested bikes' engine sizes are unknown and the standard's test conditions are not stated, so the measured 34.7 km/L (phase V) cannot be compared to 38 km/L; the paper does not draw that comparison. No g/km limits for phases III-V; no exceedance mileage.
findings.useOnSite: Check limits in TEPA sources, not this paper.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; added reason the 38 km/L comparison is unsafe.

findings.claim: Fuel economy fell with age and with mileage; the figures give r2 = 0.70 against age and r2 = 0.60 against mileage for the individual bikes.
findings.value: r2 = 0.70 (Fig. 1 inset, fuel economy vs age); r2 = 0.60 (Fig. 2 inset, fuel economy vs running mileage); phase III bikes extend to about 19 y in Fig. 1
findings.page: PDF p.4 (journal 3059) Fig. 1; PDF p.5 (journal 3060) Fig. 2
findings.quote: Fig. 1 inset 'r2=0.70'; Fig. 2 inset 'r2=0.60'
findings.caveats: Printed only in figure insets, not in the text; n=43 individual bikes; age explains somewhat more than mileage; phases overlap in both variables. No p-values.
findings.useOnSite: In this fleet, age and mileage each explained part of the variation in fuel economy (r2 0.70 and 0.60).
findings.checkerNote: Reader said no fit statistic was printed; insets show these.

findings.claim: Observed total VOC by mileage group (stacked bars, visual estimate): about 25, 26.5, 22, 27.5, 39 and 47 g/L; only the >40,000 km bar carries the significance asterisk.
findings.quote: Fig. 4 caption: 'significance versus group with mileage < 10,000 km: *p < 0.05'
findings.caveats: Values are visual estimates from the bar chart, not printed numbers. The 30-40k group (about 39 g/L) is not flagged significant in Fig. 4, though paraffins in Fig. 5(a) are flagged for 30-40k.
findings.useOnSite: Quote only the printed 47.1 g/L; use bar heights for illustration with a visual-estimate note.
findings.checkerNote: Needed to resolve the 25.2 vs 19.1 abstract/text conflict.

findings.claim: In Fig. 3 the group means are not monotonic: CO and HC dip in one mid-mileage group, so the trend is clearer for the high-mileage groups.
findings.value: Approx. group means by eye: CO about 60, 80, 95, 147, 123, 203 g/L; HC about 27, 30, 32, 28, 44, 47 g/L; NOx about 9, 7.8, 7, 7.2, 6.3, 5.4 g/L (six groups from low to high mileage)
findings.caveats: Visual estimates only. Error bars (SD) are large and overlap for neighbouring groups.
findings.useOnSite: Do not describe the rise as steady; quote the end points and the significance statement.
findings.checkerNote: Supports caution on the per-10,000 km slopes.

findings.claim: The authors say motorcycle exhaust in this work was rich in aromatics compared with light-duty car exhaust reported in another study.
findings.value: Motorcycle exhaust here: aromatics 38-48% of the measured VOC mass. Cited car data (May et al. 2014): 40% alkanes, 15% single-ring aromatics, 10% olefins/naphthenes, 25% unidentified (of non-methane organic gas).
findings.quote: a high aromatic fraction was found in motorcycle exhaust in this work
findings.caveats: Different bases (the 67 identified VOCs here vs all NMOG incl. 25% unidentified for cars), different vehicles, fuels and cycles; not a controlled comparison. Authors' explanation (high combustion efficiency, gasoline composition) is speculative.
findings.useOnSite: Cite as the authors' observation, with the comparison attributed to May et al. 2014.
findings.checkerNote: Relevant to the benzene/toluene/xylene argument but weak as a quantitative comparison.

findings.claim: The paper cites two earlier papers by the same group on motorcycle exhaust by mileage and by regulation phase; it does not say whether any data here repeat those.
findings.quote: Tsai et al. (2017a) Air pollutants and toxic emissions of various mileage motorcycles for ECE driving cycles; Tsai et al. (2017b) Criteria pollutants and volatile organic compounds emitted from motorcycle exhaust under various regulation phases
findings.caveats: Possible data overlap or reuse cannot be judged from this paper. If the site cites several Tsai papers as independent evidence, check for the same fleet.
findings.useOnSite: Do not count this paper as independent of Tsai 2017a/b without checking those papers.
findings.checkerNote: Titles are similar and the sample structure matches; paper is silent.

findings.claim: The paper tests 'motorcycles'; it does not say how many are scooters (CVT) versus manual-gear motorcycles, and electric scooters are not mentioned.

findings.claim: The paper says phase III fuel economy was 20% lower than brand-new motorcycles in the Results and that fuel consumption was 20% higher in the Conclusion; these are not the same quantity, and no new-bike baseline is shown.
findings.value: Results: 'fuel economy ... 20% lower'; Conclusion: 'fuel consumption ... 20% higher'. Within-study comparison: phase III 15% lower than phase V.
findings.quote: The fuel economy of regulation phase III motorcycles was 20% lower than that of brand-new motorcycles.
findings.caveats: The 'brand-new' reference is not defined or measured in this study (probably the 2002-2010 new-bike 36-39 km/L range cited). A 20% fall in km/L equals 25% more fuel per km, so the two statements conflict.
findings.useOnSite: Use the measured 15% (III vs V) rather than the 20% claim.
findings.checkerNote: Sceptical-reader point.

findings.claim: Mean mileages of the highest groups differ between the OFP text and the Fig. 4/5 axes.
findings.value: Text: 26,715, 36,615 and 48,917 km; Fig. 4 axis labels: 2.672, 3.623 and 4.762 x 10^4 km (and 47,617 km in the main text)
findings.caveats: Minor; indicates inconsistent group definitions or typos. Does not change conclusions.

limitations: Authors state: selected motorcycles and sample size limitation could explain non-monotonic VOC results (decrease at 15,000-20,000 km) and insignificant differences; more testing is needed for baseline information.
Authors state motorcycle emissions are affected by many factors (equipment, age/mileage, inspection and maintenance, cold/hot starts, idle fraction, temperature and humidity).
Only 43 bikes; phase III n=7; mileage groups n=6-8 each.
Cross-sectional design: mileage, age and regulation phase are confounded; bikes were not followed over time.
Emission factors per litre of fuel, not per km; no particle (PM) measurements; no 1,3-butadiene; no PAHs; Fig. 5(d) for carbonyls is cited but missing.
Lab dynamometer ECE cycle at 25-30 C with a single fuel (95 octane, 10.2% MTBE); not real-world stop-start street driving.
Engine capacities, model years, maintenance history and catalyst condition of tested motorcycles are not reported; the scooter/motorcycle split is not reported.
r2 values in Fig. 3 are from six group means.
VOC group increases with mileage are significant only for the >40,000 km group (plus 30-40k for paraffins in Fig. 5(a)).
Several numbers disagree within the paper (VOC low-mileage total 25.2 vs 19.1 g/L; phase III CO SD 71 vs 74; mean mileages of high groups).
Possible overlap with the authors' 2017a/2017b papers is not addressed.
complications: All tested vehicles are gasoline motorcycles; there are no electric scooters, no pedestrian, rider or child exposure data, no air concentrations and no health outcomes. The paper covers only chain link 1 (tailpipe) and, via OFP, a computed ozone link; it cannot support links 2, 3, 5, 6 or 7, and it never mentions electric vehicles.
NOx per litre was lower in older motorcycles (-30% phase III vs V, -41% across the mileage range) and CO2 per litre also lower.
HC difference between phase IV and V was not statistically significant.
VOC increases with mileage were significant only above 40,000 km; one mid-mileage group was lower than the lowest-mileage group.
Newest phase V motorcycles still emit about 84 g/L CO and 29 g/L HC on average; the paper compares to no limit, so it shows 'newer is better', not that new gasoline motorcycles are clean.
Benzene is among the dominant VOCs but has small ozone-forming potential and no numeric emission factor is printed; toxicity is not assessed.

The 156% CO and 84% HC figures are phase III (n=7, mean 15 y, 45,600 km) vs phase V (n=20, mean 4 y, 12,200 km) per litre of fuel; the authors attribute the difference to mileage and age, so it is confounded with wear.
Idle and cold-start effects, central to the red-light argument, are not measured separately; the paper only cites car cold-start data.
Paper says 'seven groups' of mileage but lists six.
The '20% lower fuel economy than brand-new' and '20% higher fuel consumption' statements are inconsistent and have no measured new-bike baseline.
Emission factors are per litre of fuel burned; a bike with lower fuel economy emits more per km than per-litre figures alone show, but the paper does not give per-km values.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: The +156% CO and +84% HC (phase III vs V) are per litre of fuel burned, not per km or per vehicle, from n=7 vs n=20 bikes.
The abstract also reports NOx lower (-30% phase III, -17% IV) and the full text shows CO2 per litre lower in older bikes.
Phase IV vs V HC (+9%) is not statistically significant (p>0.05).
The abstract's 25.2 +/- 8.0 g/L total VOC at low mileage agrees with Fig. 4 (about 25) but not the body text (19.1 +/- 9.7); the rise to 47.1 is significant only for the >40,000 km group.
Abstract names benzene among main VOCs but no benzene emission factor is printed; no 1,3-butadiene; carbonyls are 1.8-3.0% of VOC mass.
No emission limits or exceedance mileage are given.
The paper has no idle-specific, pedestrian, exposure or health content.
Table 1 prints integers for HC and different precision from the text (e.g. NOx 5.57 vs 5.6).

answersToQuestions: 1. Design: 43 in-use four-stroke gasoline motorcycles in Taiwan (7 phase III, 16 phase IV, 20 phase V; mean ages 15.0/8.2/4.0 y; mean mileages 45,613/30,120/12,179 km; phases phased in 1998-2003, 2004-2007, 2007-2017). Model years and engine sizes of the tested bikes are not given; scooter vs manual-gear split not given. Six mileage groups (text says seven): 0-10,000 n=6; 10,001-15,000 n=8; 15,001-20,000 n=8; 20,001-30,000 n=8; 30,001-40,000 n=6; >40,001 n=7. ECE cycle 780 s (240 s idle, 168 s acceleration, 228 s cruise at 30 and 50 km/h, 144 s deceleration); WMTC not mentioned; cold start is not stated for this test (fuel replaced and engine cooled overnight). Room 25-30 C; 95-octane fuel with 10.2% MTBE, 30.0 vol% aromatics, 0.52% benzene. HORIBA CVS-51S dilution tunnel with bag sampling over the whole cycle; NDIR (CO, CO2), FID (THC), chemiluminescence (NOx); purge-and-trap GC/MS (52 VOCs) and DNPH-HPLC (15 carbonyls); OFP from Carter (2009) MIR; two-way ANOVA with Scheffe test, p<0.05.

2. Emission factors are per litre of fuel (not per km). Phase III/IV/V: CO 216/125/84.3 g/L; HC 54.0/32.1/29.4; NOx 5.57/6.64/7.96; CO2 1838/1979/2098; fuel economy 29.5/32.6/34.7 km/L (Table 1, PDF p.4; Table 1 prints III CO SD 71, text 74). By mileage group only the end points are printed (CO 61 to 203, HC 27 to 47, NOx 9.1 to 5.4 g/L; fuel economy 35.5 to 29.9 km/L); the six group means appear only in Fig. 3 (CO about 60, 80, 95, 147, 123, 203; HC about 27, 30, 32, 28, 44, 47 by eye). No g/km values and no table by mileage group.

3. No species-by-mileage table. Printed: paraffins 9.0-19, olefins 2.2-5.7, aromatics 8.9-22, carbonyls 0.41-0.80 g/L (text low-end values disagree with the figure bars); group shares paraffins 38-45%, olefins 9.7-15%, aromatics 38-48%, carbonyls 1.8-3.0%; total 67 VOCs 47.1 +/- 19.8 g/L at 47,617 km (25.2 abstract / 19.1 text at 5,231 km). Dominant species: aromatics toluene, m,p-xylene, o-xylene, trimethylbenzenes, m-ethyltoluene, ethylbenzene, benzene (68-79% of aromatics); paraffins isopentane, n-pentane, 2,3-dimethylbutane, 3-methylpentane, n-decane, n-undecane; olefins 1-butene, propene, isoprene, 1-hexene (70-82%); carbonyls formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone, butyraldehyde, benzaldehyde, isovaleraldehyde, valeraldehyde (78-84%). Benzene is a thin segment in Fig. 5(c) (about 0.7-1 g/L by eye, not a printed value). 1,3-butadiene not reported; formaldehyde mass not printed (OFP 0.47-1.18 g-O3/L). Fig. 5(d) is cited but absent.

4. Deterioration (cross-sectional, per litre of fuel, 5,231 to 47,617 km): CO 61 to 203 g/L (3.3-fold; 34 g/L per 10,000 km; r2 0.87); HC 27 to 47 g/L (1.7-fold; 4.7 g/L per 10,000 km; r2 0.80; significant above 30,000 km); NOx 9.1 to 5.4 g/L (-41%; -0.87 g/L per 10,000 km; r2 0.89); fuel economy 35.5 to 29.9 km/L (-16%; about 1.3 km/L per 10,000 km; Fig. 2 inset r2 0.60); 67 VOCs +6.61 g/L per 10,000 km, significant only above 40,000 km. The paper gives no limits and does not say at what mileage emissions exceed any standard.

5. OFP (computed): 67 VOCs 105, 109, 91, 111, 174, 204 g-O3/L across the six mileage groups (Table 2); 1.95-fold rise; 23.4 g-O3/L per 10,000 km. Shares: aromatics 50-67%, olefins 22-34% (table 21-34%), paraffins 10-13%, carbonyls 2-3%. Top species (averages): 1-butene 13.7, m,p-xylene 13.0, isoprene 11.7, toluene 10.5, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene 10.3, o-xylene 9.6 g-O3/L. Benzene is not among the 20 species tabulated.

6. Idle: the cycle has 240 s idle, but no idle-only results. Cold start: Taiwan's test changed from hot to cold start in January 2004; the paper cites May et al. 2014 (cars) for 5-10 times higher NMHC at cold start; no cold-start result of its own. Catalyst ageing: only the suggestion that HC rise above 30,000 km 'may be attributed to incomplete combustion and failure of the catalyst system'; not tested. Maintenance: not measured; the paper lists inspection and maintenance among factors and describes annual inspection for bikes older than five years.

7. The paper cites no CO/HC/NOx g/km limits for any phase. It gives phase periods (III 1998-2003, IV 2004-2007, V 2007-2017, phase VI following Euro 4 as of 2017), Taiwan fuel-economy standards (36 and 39 km/L 2002-2010; 38 km/L from 2011 for 100-150 cc) and guaranteed mileage (6,000 km 1991; 15,000 km 1998; 20,000 km 2017). It also claims Taiwan has 'the toughest motorcycle emission standards in the world' without a citation.

8. Conclusions (PDF p.9-10): 'The fuel consumption of regulation phase III motorcycles was found to be 20% higher than that the brand-new motorcycles.' and 'The results indicate that motorcycle fuel economy decreased with increasing age and running mileage.' They give per-10,000 km deterioration rates (CO 34, HC 4.7, NOx -0.87, VOC +6.61 g/L; OFP +23.4 g-O3/L). No explicit recommendation on inspection, retirement or scrapping of old motorcycles and none on electric vehicles. Nearest statements: Results p.3060 'more motorcycle exhaust emission testing is required to obtain baseline information for the development of motorcycle air pollution control strategies'; abstract 'The implementation of control measures for motorcycles in urban areas depends on the establishment of baseline measures'; Introduction: periodic inspection and maintenance tests 'require consumers to perform repairs to reduce emissions'.
